reference.source: Standard endocrinology reference texts and primary aldosteronism consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A surgically curable cause of secondary hypertension, classically presenting with hypertension and spontaneous or diuretic-provoked hypokalaemia, though many patients are normokalaemic
The biochemical signature is autonomous aldosterone excess with suppressed renin, giving a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio as the screening test
Confirmatory testing demonstrates non-suppressible aldosterone (e.g. saline infusion or salt-loading) to distinguish true aldosteronism from other causes
Somatic mutations in ion channels and pumps, particularly KCNJ5, are common drivers of autonomous aldosterone secretion in these adenomas
Adrenal vein sampling is the reference standard to lateralise aldosterone hypersecretion and separate unilateral adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia before surgery
Cross-sectional imaging alone is unreliable because small adenomas may be missed and coincidental non-functioning nodules can mislead
Unilateral disease is treated with laparoscopic adrenalectomy, whereas bilateral or non-surgical cases are managed with mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonism
reference.pathophysiology: An aldosterone-producing adenoma is a benign cortical tumour, usually arising in the zona glomerulosa, that autonomously secretes aldosterone independent of the renin-angiotensin system. Somatic mutations affecting ion transport (for example in the KCNJ5 potassium channel, or in calcium-handling genes) depolarise glomerulosa cells, increase intracellular calcium and drive constitutive aldosterone synthase activity. Excess aldosterone promotes renal sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, producing volume-dependent hypertension, a tendency to hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, and suppression of renin. Chronic mineralocorticoid excess also causes target-organ damage disproportionate to the blood pressure.
additionalDifferentials: Liddle syndrome and other apparent mineralocorticoid excess states
additionalInvestigations: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio as the initial screen, with attention to interfering antihypertensive drugs
Confirmatory suppression testing (saline infusion or oral salt loading) to prove autonomous aldosterone secretion
Serum potassium, acid-base status and assessment of end-organ damage
Adrenal CT to characterise nodules and exclude carcinoma
Adrenal vein sampling to lateralise the source before surgery
Genetic testing for familial hyperaldosteronism in young patients or those with a family history
redFlags: Severe or resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia raising concern for significant mineralocorticoid excess
Profound hypokalaemia causing arrhythmia or muscle weakness
A large or radiologically atypical adrenal mass suggesting carcinoma rather than a benign adenoma
Hypertensive target-organ damage disproportionate to blood pressure level
reference.prognosis: Unilateral adenomas are often cured or substantially improved by adrenalectomy, with normalisation of potassium and improvement in blood pressure, though long-standing hypertension may persist and require ongoing therapy. Untreated primary aldosteronism carries excess cardiovascular and renal risk relative to matched essential hypertension.
pitfalls: Screening while on interfering drugs (e.g. mineralocorticoid antagonists) that invalidate the aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Relying on CT appearances alone and operating on the wrong side without adrenal vein sampling
Missing normokalaemic primary aldosteronism by only testing hypertensive patients with low potassium
Failing to replace potassium and control blood pressure before surgery
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on primary aldosteronism
